newsitem.title: GERMANY: 12-year-old actor wows Berlin Film Festival.
newsitem.headline: 12-year-old actor wows Berlin Film Festival.

text.p: Twelve-year-old British actor Jordan Kiziuk enthralled the Berlin Film Festival on Wednesday with a cinema debut performance as a small Jewish boy who survives a Polish ghetto during World War Two.

As the star of "The Island on Bird Street," which had its premiere at the 47th annual festival, Kiziuk plays a bright child whose luck and ingenuity keep him alive despite constant raids on the ghetto by Nazi SS men.

He fronts an international cast which includes Hollywood veteran Jack Warden and Irish star Patrick Bergin, but the boy from Lancashire, England, who was 11 when he played the part of Alex, acts alone during most of the 100-minute epic.

"It was difficult having one boy carrying the film completely," Danish director Soren Kragh-Jacobsen said. "We saw hundreds of 10-year-old boys, but there came Mr. Jordan Kiziuk and he stole my heart."
Kiziuk, who had only appeared in theatre and dance productions before, said that history classes in school had helped prepare him for the challenge of playing the young Alex.
"I studied history at school and I learned how people were killed (in the Holocaust)," Kiziuk said after the film's screening. "So I knew how much to be frightened of what was happening."
The Nazis systematically separated the Jewish populations across eastern Europe and interned them in barbed-wire and brick-enclosed ghettos.
There they were subjected to notorious "selections" to decide who would be sent to the death camps or stay on as slave labourers for German industry.
Alex's father Stefan, played by Bergin in the film, promises his son that he will return for him in the ghetto when they are separated by Nazi troops.

"This is the story of a brave boy who nearly lies down to die because he thought he had nothing more to live for," Kiziuk said. "Then he heard his father's voice and only that could bring him back to life."

Kragh-Jacobsen, who started his career making children's films, called his picture "not just another a Holocaust story" and said that it bore special relevance today because what he described as a lack of trust between generations.
"Sometimes I feel we are living in a faithless age," the director said. "People don't keep their promises, and that is something I think parents should never do to their kids."
The film adapts the book of the same title by Uri Orlev, who wrote of his experiences in the Warsaw Ghetto as a child. Orlev now lives in Israel with his wife and four children.
"Mr Orlev said there were only two things he remembered about that time," Kragh-Joacobsen said. "One was the silence -- he said it was so silent all the time.

"The second was feathers," he said, explaining the title of the book and the film. "He always remembered feathers, because of looters who cut up pillows to find leftovers (in the empty apartments of the ghetto)."
